subtopic: PREFERENCE IN PURCHASE OF CANADIAN PRODUCTS
PREFERENCE IN PURCHASE OF CANADIAN PRODUCTS
speechtext:
1.	Does the Canadian Government Supply Services follow a policy favouring the purchase of Canadian products and, if so, what are the particulars of such policy?
2.	What was the total amount of purchases by these services during the last fiscal year and of that amount, what proportion was (a) for Canadian products (b) for foreign products?
3.	Does the government intend to propose the enactment of legislation similar to the "Buy American Act" and, if not, for what reasons?

Hon. James Richardson (Minister of Supply
and Services): In so far as the Department of Supply and Services is concerned: 1. The policy of the department with regard to the purchase of Canadian products is, as reflected in the general conditions that are applicable
to departmental contracts, that to the full extent to which they are procurable, consistent with proper economy and the expeditious carrying out of the contract, Canadian labour, parts and materials shall be used. Therefore, the department buys from Canadian firms if practicable and only turns to other sources of supply when procurement from the Canadian sources is deemed to be uneconomical or impractical.
In addition, it is the government's policy that a modest premium will be paid for a product with higher Canadian content. This premium is calculated at up to 10% of the difference of foreign content.
2.	The total net value of the contractual documents issued by the Department of Supply and Services during the fiscal year 1968-1969 was $861,152,000.
In high value equipments such as aircraft, ships, special vehicles, etcetera, due to agreements for defence production sharing with the United States and other NATO countries, many components contain an element of foreign content, but on an overall procurement basis, by far the largest proportion is Canadian. Due to the difficulty of tracing the relative Canadian and foreign content through all sub-contract levels, and the high cost which would be involved in maintaining separate accounts for this purpose, such records are not kept.
3.	No. It is not considered in Canada's overall interest to introduce restrictive legislation of this type, because of the protection already afforded Canadian industry by present import duties, together with the provision for paying a premium for Canadian content.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. W. Groos (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: RETRAINING FOR RETIRING ARMED SERVICES PERSONNEL
speechtext:
1. Yes.
2. The program, called "The Civilian Employment Assistance Program", is a joint effort of the Department of National Defence and the Department of Manpower and Immigration. The scope of the program includes counselling by the Canadian Forces Personnel Selection Officer in the areas of evaluation

of work interests, including the use of objective psychological measures, evaluation of military training and experience as related to civilian employment, assistance in planning academic upgrading prior to retirement and current information about the civilian labour market. He also provides assistance in the preparation of a career resume and a maximum of 20 printed and bound copies, complete with photo portrait, are provided at no cost to the individual. Under the provision of Bill C-278 "The Adult Occupation Training Act" individuals whose skills and experience do not qualify them for satisfactory entry into the civilian labour force may be provided with suitable occupational training. The need for such training is initiated and assessed by the designated Manpower counsellor responsible for retiring servicemen in co-operation with the military Personnel Selection Officer. Assistance is provided, both on a local and nation wide basis, by the local Manpower counsellor towards available job opportunities best suited to an individual's particular needs; or develop job opportunities for an individual by bringing his qualifications to the attention of potential employers.
3.	Formal courses of instructions are not offered within the service, but the program offers counselling in academic upgrading and preparation for occupational retraining, as managed by the Department of Manpower and Immigration.
4.	The program is designed primarily for all long service personnel who will be released upon reaching compulsory release age. It is also available to personnel upon termination of a short service commission or who are being released prematurely (honourably, and for other than voluntary reasons), except that for those released with less than ten years service, DND limits its responsibilities to that of providing a counselling service. Entry to the program for those eligible is voluntary and can commence five years before retirement.
5.	The text of the pertinent order, CFAO 5620, is published once each quarter in unit orders. Articles describing the program have been published in the Armed Forces Magazine "The Sentinel", a poster has been printed and distributed to all Bases in Canada and locations overseas, articles and regular news columns have been printed in garrison and unit newspapers, as well as newspapers such as the Financial Post. In addition, the letter sent to senior personnel, advising them of the
June 11. 1969

6.	The military contribution to this program has been in existence in differing forms, on individual basis, since 1958, and on an integrated basis since March 1965. The Department of Manpower and Immigration joined in on January 1, 1968.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I started last night to make a few remarks on the budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). This budget is certainly not an innovation, but rather a repetition of the Canadian economic adventure we have been living for a hundred years,, that is: an increase in expenditures, the impossibility to reduce taxes and the necessity of increasing production.

In other words, it is the same old story that is being repeated, while 68 per cent of the workers earn less than $4,000 a year.
Last night, an amendment to an amendment was brought before the house with a view to drawing attention to people earning $4,000 or less a year, and that matter does not seem to have been dealt with seriously. That is why I wish to come back to it.
We are facing two problems. There are in Canada two classes of people who can keep pace neither with prosperity nor with the rise in the cost of living. They are the 470,000 unemployed and the 4 million workers earning less than $4,000 a year.
There is another category to which I particularly want to draw the attention of hon. members; it is the mass of young workers, 18 to 27 years old, who come on the labour market for some time, or who are unemployed.
About two weeks ago, a convention called "Carrefour 69" was held in Montreal. On that occasion, thousands of young people met, not revolutionaries or protesters, but young people who were asking themselves whether it is possible to have a place in society without depriving the neighbour of his. They were asking themselves whether it is possible for them to have a family and to earn a living as everybody else, and so on.
Mr. Speaker, during the whole week-end, I heard, while attending that meeting, extremely convincing comments about the present economic situation and the efficiency of the present economic system. During that convention "Carrefour 69", I was struck by many things, namely a closed circuit television program during which young people were interviewed. Each time they were asked: What are you doing at "Carrefour 69"? What is your problem? What is your name?
To the question "What is your problem" many just showed their wallet containing an identity card, an unemployment insurance card as well as a driving licence. That is all we have, said those youngsters, and our problem is that we can only have in our wallet that famous unemployment insurance card.
Those young people are 22, 23, 24 or 25 years old. They want to work. They are ready to work and to do something for their country, their province, their municipality, for themselves, but we are not organized economically, not only at the national but also at the provincial levels, to put to use those prodigious skills which are lost.
June 11. 1969

Nearly 5,000 young people attended "Car-refour 69" and more than 90 per cent of them carried an unemployment insurance card in their pockets. Those are our children, our youth, the best labour force we could find, in good health, full of good will and ready to work. However, governments are unable to give them that opportunity.
Mr. Speaker, invitations had been sent out to Ottawa and Quebec ministers who are particularly concerned with this problem, and who are supposed, on account of their activities in the parliamentary, legislative and ministerial fields, to be interested in such matters. Those ministers did not even acknowledge the invitations to "Carrefour 69" sent out by over 10,000 young people.
It is a shame. Do you know how many hon. members were present? All were invited and there was only one. I, your humble servant, was there and I do not boast about it. I felt almost ashamed to be there alone, I felt like a lost soul among those young people eager to work but who have nobody to listen to them. Tomorrow, if they send a brief to Quebec or Ottawa, this will be the reply: We thank you for your very good brief. It is very well documented, some of your ideas are excellent but, dear young people, future voters, you will realize the situation. In fact, the good old politicians want to pat them on the back because they want their votes, but they tell them: Keep quiet, we are looking for solutions, we have tremendous plans, we have instituted a study committee on the stabilization of prices. We are in the process of reviewing the policy concerning unemployment insurance and manpower centres. Just keep quiet. Do not upset anything, do not break anything. Stay at home, remain unemployed and spend your unemployment insurance cheque. When you have nothing left, go to the welfare office and you will be given a third card. This is quite a step forward for a young 23-year-old individual. He goes to the welfare office and says: I have used up all my unemployment insurance stamps. Could I have a welfare card?
Mr. Speaker, many of the young people who attended "Carrefour 69" had only two cards in their pockets to identify themselves: the unemployment insurance card and the welfare card. They have no driving license as they cannot afford it. They cannot afford a car either.
Mr. Speaker, we would like those young people, who will make up the society of
The Budget-Mr. Fortin tomorrow, who will be the leaders of tomorrow, who represent also our best manpower, as they are healthy and want to work, to stay home and say: Canada is tremendous, Quebec is tremendous, the Liberal party is tremendous! We do not change anything.
Mr. Speaker, if we do not give work to those young people today-I do not necessarily mean bread and butter on their table-we shall wake up tomorrow face to face with a society that will be out of control. However, our economic system is organized in such a way that economic blood does not circulate through it. Indeed, money does not circulate or does only for the stronger and the wealthier people, so that production cannot be disposed of on account of the people's lack of purchasing power. Thus, there is no need to renew our production stock and the unemployment rate increases.
To tolerate 470,000 unemployed people in a country as wealthy as ours is a real scandal. It is the more scandalous when we know the majority of the unemployed population is made up of young people.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw the attention of the hon. members to the fact that this matter should be studied seriously. We have all it takes, in Canada, to build a great country, to enable everyone to live and develop properly; but absolutely nothing is being done.
Committees are set up to study reports of other committees and, in our offices, in our libraries, there are big books which cost millions of dollars dealing with these problems but they gather dust on the shelves. That does not change anything. In the meantime, the unemployed stroll along with their hands in their pockets, with their unemployment and welfare cards. Talk about a future for those young people!
Mr. Speaker, to my mind this situation is absolutely intolerable and unacceptable; something must be done to change it. What astonishes me most in all that, which I fail to understand, is that when we introduced the non-confidence motion which read as follows:
That, in the opinion of the house, the government has failed to take adequate measures in order to give Canadians the benefit of a policy of distribution of goods and services which would allow each citizen to obtain his share of Canadian abundance.
Instead of getting replies to our assertions, we had to put up with jokes. Hon. members found it funny that such a motion should be moved. Yesterday similar motions were moved

June 11, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Fortin and again it was funny. They think everything is funny, Mr. Speaker.
When the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) endeavoured to reply to the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) about the motion I have just mentioned, he said that Social Credit was a doctrine that could not be implemented, that it was not sound, that it was a machine to make money, that we indulged in demagoguery because we were speaking of poverty, because we were defending the workers, the small people against the rich.
But when the minister was a labour leader-I hope he still remembers,, because his attitude gives the impression that he has forgotten-he was stirring up the small guys, the workers, for his own purposes and his own interests, not those of the union members. At that time, he was using demagoguery, and he was the first one to criticize governments for their lack of action and activity.
Today, he is the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. His department is supposed to make funds available to the people to achieve the accelerated development of some regions with a slow economic growth. The minister should be particularly interested in these questions, but he is not in the house now, and all he can do when we propose solutions is make fun of us.
On the other hand, this same minister stands up and says: We wish to accuse the opposition of not co-operating, because it does not want to study the government proposals. This same minister does not have the intellectual decency to practise what he preaches. If he wants us to study his proposals, he should at least have the decency to examine ours and to stop ridiculing them without first having examined them seriously.
Mr. Speaker, Social Credit surely represents an avant-garde doctrine. It proposes some very interesting economic and monetary measures which are neither socialistic nor necessarily capitalistic. Capitalism, at the present time, is abusive. Social Credit is a doctrine which can go well with the capitalist system; according to the Creditiste system, all human beings are equal and they all have, regardless of their age, their colour, their race, their religion, the right to live and to grow healthily and humanly.
According to the Social Credit doctrine, money should serve man, instead of man serving money.

We do not indulge in demagoguery; we do not make fun of the people or of governments. We have been elected for a specific purpose: to try to make it clear to the government that Social Credit may have good things to offer, which it might be worth while to consider seriously, and which should not be mocked, because they might offer some efficient solutions which would restore the balance of the economic and monetary system.
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly not Social Credit that created the present economic crisis and inflation, nor those we experienced in the past.
As a matter of fact, this economic system is precisely the one that causes these crises, and those who suffer from them are, of course, the Canadian citizens. That is why the Social Credit party suggests that we attack the real problem that always makes Canadians victims of these economic crises willed by financiers, because they serve their interests as wars do.
We want to put some order there. We do not claim to have all the light from the Holy Spirit as the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion said the other day, while everything on the minister's side is in the dark. If we look at the attitude taken by the members opposite, I feel that even if we do not have all the light, it is certainly not to be found on the opposite side, because they do not even bother to consider our proposals.
Mr. Speaker, I think that they should have the decency to consider our proposal when we say, for instance, that we should find a balance between production and consumption.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
To me, that goes without saying. But the only thing the government has to say about this is that production should be increased.
To produce more, we must first dispose of present production. Do we have enough purchasing power for this? As a matter of fact, one cannot buy with prayers and electoral promises, as the government does, but one needs purchasing power, scriptural or other credit. If the taxpayer does not have any credit and if we keep picking his pockets, how can this production be got rid of in order that more production may be possible?
Obviously, if goods remain on the shelves, workers will not find any jobs producing more goods to replace the unsold ones.
We prefer to play into the hands of high finance. That is what happened in wartime when butter was thrown away, when a lot of
June 11. 1969

commodities were wasted while two thirds of the world were starving to death. That is what we did instead of asking ourselves if people could not consume that production through sufficient purchasing power or at least through an annual guaranteed income allowing them to dispose of it.
There would be so many things to say about this matter. As to Social credit, however, we think that we could find really interesting solutions by organizing a round table to consider such possibilities. We strongly believe in this, but we wish the Minister of Finance and his colleague would examine those solutions.
We are ready to co-operate, but not to be ridiculed. We wish our proposals were not brushed aside but studied seriously.
Mr. Speaker, we often say that we are ready to co-operate; however we would like that co-operation not to be a unilateral endeavour, but to proceed from a real sense of dialogue.
I hope that my honourable colleagues in their debates will not forget all those young workers who would be very pleased to have a job but who, at the present time, are not in a position to work or to throw themselves into a career. Then, they should not be blamed if they do not take part in our economic life. The governments do not co-operate with all those workers who would be only too pleased to help build this country, provided they were given an opportunity to do so.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Pierre Cote (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like in the first place to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) who has used to the full his imagination and his intelligence to present to the Canadian people a realistic as well as a popular budget-which is surely not easy- and especially to realize a budgetary surplus, the first since 1956.
He wanted, through that budget, to control inflation by using all available resources.
To fight that inflation, the Minister of Finance has taken certain steps aimed at intensifying price competition. By grouping the three last stages of tariff reductions provided under the Kennedy round, the Minister of Finance wanted to control the increase in consumer prices.
The budget will also make it possible to allow more substantial exemptions for goods brought back by Canadians from abroad and will allow a Canadian, on a verbal statement,
The Budget-Mr. Fortin to bring back $5 worth of goods each time he goes through custom. Those changes were welcomed by the public in general and the Department of National Revenue, notably as far as the Customs Division is concerned, because they will facilitate and improve service at customs.
The other measures in the budget, which I have not yet mentioned, are parts of a whole which, while fighting inflation, can be related to the general policy of the Canadian government to eliminate regional disparities.

I should like to make a few comments about the changes in the customs tariff contained in the recent budget resolutions. Firstly, there is acceleration of the Kennedy round reductions, which has the effect of implementing, effective June 4, 1969, the rates of duty which were scheduled to take effect on January 1, 1972, except with respect to one item covering shoeboard. This created an initial flurry of requests from field offices and interested parties for confirmation and clarification. These new rates are now being applied and as they become known it is anticipated that they will not create any abnormal administrative problems.
Secondly, certain recommendations of the tariff board with respect to three references have been implemented. These are reference No. 133, dealing with machinery, apparatus, printing plates and related products for the printing and allied industries; reference No. 134, dealing with equipment for hospitals and other institutions, and reference No. 138, dealing with certain precision instruments and apparatus.
These changes will require extensive review and adjustment of our previous administrative practices. It is anticipated that many requests for explanations of these new items and for the updating of rulings will be received. Some printed directives will require revision. No unforeseen administrative difficulties are expected.
Thirdly, there are certain amendments which are in the nature of housekeeping changes. For example, certain articles are excluded from items 41525-1 and 44300-1. This will permit Canadian users of industrial sewing machines and certain cooking apparatus to benefit under the duty remission program known as the machinery program, which is administered by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Also included in this group is provision for extension of
June 11, 1969

The Budget-Hon. J.-P. Cote the duty free importation of aircraft and aircraft engines of types and sizes not made in Canada. Again, while these changes will require review of past practices, together with correction and adjustment of rulings, records and administrative approaches, no special difficulties are expected.
In the customs tariff new provisions have been introduced that will be of benefit to residents of Canada when they return from visits outside the country. All of these provisions have been designed in the interest of facilitating the movement of the returning resident through customs and generally to provide a more generous, more practical and more frequent exemption privilege for Canadian travellers. For instance, on goods other than tobacco products and alcoholic beverages that accompany the traveller in his baggage upon his return after an absence of 48 hours or more, there is an exemption granted on the strength of a verbal declaration alone in an amount not to exceed $5 on any number of occasions.
Effective next January 1 the regular privileges will be on the basis of one $25 exemption, including specified amounts of tobacco products and alcoholic beverages, after an absence of 48 hours, during each calendar quarter of the year. As well, there will be an additional privilege of one $100 exemption in each calendar year after an absence of 12 days in any country outside of Canada. This includes, for the first time, the United States. This exemption will include the same quantities of tobacco products and alcoholic beverages. Beyond this, goods imported in excess of these limits up to a value of $100 will be subject to a flat or common rate of 25 per cent except in the case of tobacco products and alcoholic beverages accompanying the returning resident. This latter privilege is being made immediately available. While the benefits of the increased frequency of exemptions and the broader application of the $100 privilege will be welcomed by Canadian residents, the $5 verbal declaration and flat rate features will serve to expedite the passage of travellers through customs. Officers of my department also see these changes as a practical step in further facilitating the movement of travellers entering our country.

As for the Income Tax Division of the Department of National Revenue, it might be interesting for hon. members, at this time of the year, to know where we stand in respect

of the income tax returns received so far this year.
May I first say that we have received up to June 9, 1969, 8,513,792 tax returns, which is about 400,000 more than last year. Out of this total, 6,640,113 have been assessed, and 4,779,070 refunds sent out, which means that by May 31, 1969, we had checked a million returns more than last year.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
[English}
In as much as I am the minister responsible for collecting the revenue sought to be raised by the Income Tax Act, I would like to take this opportunity of explaining to members of the house the philosophy in the compliance aspects which I requested my deputy minister to operate within so as to ensure that all taxpayers in Canada are treated in an equitable and fair manner. It became readily apparent to me that some of the past policies by which my department was governed were not now applicable to the changing circumstances existing today.
Let it not be said that we are concerned only with ourselves and our own efficiency. I have given much thought to the need for equitable treatment among taxpayers. One area that has been explored is the collection of outstanding taxes. Each year a number of our citizens and corporations owe taxes, and admit they do, but fail to pay up when the tax is due. This imposes a burden on the country and other taxpayers and the department has been quite efficient in taking strong action on these delinquents. However, I have become concerned that taxpayers who make an attempt to question their assessments or who pay even a token amount on receipt of the notice, may be treated no differently from those who ignore us completely. These people may be subject to garnishees and writs without regard to whether there was a response from them.
Although I see no remedy other than our present practices in dealing with taxpayers who ignore our routine requests for payment, I expect that reasonable judgment will be used before issuing garnishees against taxpayers owing small amounts. But for the others, I have directed that no taxpayer who responds to an assessment notice or collection letter will be proceeded against by garnishment or writ until he has been contacted by telephone and personally interviewed or advised in writing that a satisfactory solution to the non-payment is being sought. Only if
June 11. 1969	COMMONS
an agreement cannot be reached will garnishees or writs be issued.
One particular policy which existed for some years was that of selective prosecutions; that is, only certain cases from the many investigated were prosecuted. Why should we proceed against one man and not against the other? This, I felt, was a most difficult policy to administer because of the difficulty of achieving uniformity of treatment. I, therefore, directed my departmental officers to administer the act on the basis of the existing facts in any case and the law applicable to those facts. This I am certain will ensure fair and equitable treatment to all taxpayers.
I might add that despite the high level of taxes, the vast majority of taxpayers are honest when filing their income tax returns. However, there is a minority in all segments of the community who are prepared to resort to dishonesty and fraud in order to escape their proper share of the income tax burden and, hence, impose upon the honest taxpayer an ever increasing share. Some people do not have their tax deducted at source and think they can decide how much tax they will pay. They file false receipts or do not disclose income.
This minority apparently regards tax evasion as a game or a sport to be played with the tax collector. I am determined that my department bring home to this minority the fact that tax evasion is not a game, that the fraud practised in connection with a source of revenue has precisely the same effect as if the evader had robbed the cashier in the income tax office. I think you will all agree that tax evasion is a despicable crime against the whole community because it takes money out of the pocket of every honest man and often out of the pockets of those who can least afford it. The courts have stated that tax evasion or the filing of false returns is a serious criminal offence and, accordingly, I would expect that the courts will impose penalties that are appropriate to the circumstances on this minority as an effective deterrent. My department's policy is to investigate every suspected fraud and in future to prosecute in very case where the evidence will support a criminal action. This policy is designed to bring home to those who would play the evasion game the consequences of their act, namely, prosecution. In this way, it is hoped that these prosecutions will act as a deterrent to others who might be contemplating tax evasion. Under this policy
The Budget-Hon. J.-P. Cote these people should bear in mind the consequences of their acts when they are contemplating fraud because it will be too late to plead ignorance once the crime has been detected by my department.
In the interests of justice, the department's prosecution policy must and will be based on the facts and evidence of the crime and it will not take into account the prominence, the influence or the position in the community of the taxpayers under investigation. Even if I have the ministerial discretion under the act I will not, where the facts indicate it, interfere in any way whatsoever with the decision reached by my departmental officials and I can assure you that my department will not place itself in the role of judge and jury but will leave the judgment of these offenders to the criminal courts. I consider tax fraud far too serious a matter to settle cases on an out-of-court basis. None of these cases have been settled or will be settled in my office.
However, I would like to assure the members of this house that I have requested all employees in my department, in so far as is humanly possible, to treat all taxpayers in an equitable and fair manner. At the same time, employees are to be reasonable in dealing with all taxpayers, no matter what their circumstances may be. You will realize the department can only gain and keep the respect of the tax paying public, which is essential to proper tax administration, so long as it acts in a fair but firm manner.
Along with this firm approach I wish to assure all members of the house that any member of the tax paying public who has been playing this game of tax evasion, but who comes forth to the department before the department takes any action concerning his file, can settle up his affairs with the department by paying the proper liability under the act without fear of prosecution. This has been the policy practised by the department in the past but it has not been widely known. I can assure you that if taxpayers do come forth voluntarily and pay their liability, they will not be prosecuted. It is my desire that taxpayers voluntarily comply, as this procedure costs the government less than having to seek out this minority who refuse to pay their fair share of the national burden. It is my desire and aim that the policy will always be such as to make voluntary compliance as easy as possible.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not taken part in a budget debate for several years. I wish to
June 11, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Fairweather talk about three or four matters I consider urgent. The government, through the medium of the budget or other institutions1, has not taken concerted action on these matters and therefore I ask for a few minutes in which to state the issues. Since the budget was a monumental yawn, I suppose the budget debate is in danger of being considered boring. I will take my chances on that, Mr. Speaker.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Matters that come to my mind under government initiative, not only in the constituency of Fundy-Royal and in the Atlantic provinces, but in the broader perspective of all Canada, are as follows: First, available shipbuilding policy; second, measures to assist the serious condition faced by dairy farmers in this country; third, a flexible policy of availability of bank loans throughout the country and fourth, a genuine and concerted attack on the mounting problem of pollution.
With regard to the first problem, that of shipbuilding policy, it was my privilege just last Saturday to attend the christening of two supply ships for the navy at the Saint John Shipbuilding and Dry-dock Company. It was a most interesting experience of co-operation between the workmen involved and the management of the dock. I am informed that the vessels are the largest order ever placed by the government of Canada for shipbuilding in the history of this country. They were built on a fixed contract, which may be of interest to those who had anything to do with the H.M.C.S. Bonaventure. An equally important feature of this construction was that they were within two weeks of the timetable set out in the contract. This is a remarkable achievement of shipbuilding skill and ability. It is one that I am rather proud to say took place in constituencies co-represented, if there is such an expression, by the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) and myself.
During the ceremonies last Saturday, the Chairman of the shipbuilding and drydock company spoke to those present, including the New Brunswick representative in the cabinet, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Dube). I now wish to quote from the remarks of the Chairman:
It is a day when we have an opportunity to see the results of many long months of effort by the men who possess the skills to build such ships, and to these men I would take this opportunity to pay special tribute. These skills are a tradition in Saint John, and it is in Saint John's interest, New

Brunswick's interest, and in the interest of Canada that these skills be preserved and used to advantage in the future.
It is because this is a national problem and not a local one that I feel no hesitation in bringing this issue before this parliament in the traditional way, that is by taking part in the budget debate. The Chairman went on to say:
If these skills are to be preserved and if we are to continue to build great ships then Canada must very soon establish a clearcut shipbuilding policy. This fact has been recognized-and perhaps I should say finally recognized-by the government of Canada.
The Chairman then referred to a statement made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) regarding a year-long study into the market for a privately owned merchant fleet. The minister described this as a necessary prelude to any further study of the possibility of building deepsea vessels in Canada to form a merchant marine. The Chairman said:
The minister, therefore, presumably is talking about a delay of up to two years before any shipbuilding and merchant marine program can be developed.
There is no shipyard in Canada that can stand this type of delay in enunciation of government policy. We need only witness the shipyard closures within the past months along the St. Lawrence River. The Chairman further states:
That is too long. In New Brunswick we cannot wait two years. Certainly, we welcome the step taken by the minister-and we recognize he has only just recently taken over this important portfolio-but Ottawa should take immediate steps to assure that existing shipyards will survive while these studies are taking place.
At this shipyard we will support any plan which will help in the development of a positive shipbuilding policy-and I feel confident in saying that management and labour will work together to achieve this goal-
It was remarkable that at the christening last Saturday the words of the Chairman were echoed by the representatives of the main trade union groups working in the shipyard, that is, Mr. Armstrong, Mr. McLeod and Mr. Yeomans. I am not a special pleader for any specific group. That would be unbecoming the role of a member of parliament, but I consider that after five or six years this government has had sufficient time to come to a decision about whether they feel this country, with the longest coastline of any nation on earth, should have as a complement to this geographical fact some policy toward a deep-sea fleet.
June 11, 1969	COMMONS
The second matter, Mr. Speaker, is of interest not only to many of my constituents, but to Canadians who do not live in the industrial heartland of the country. It concerns the crisis being faced by the dairy industry in Canada. I welcome the decision of the Standing Committee on Agriculture to move about the country. They are now in Ontario, having returned from the Atlantic provinces. It is a useful exercise for parliamentary committees to get outside this chamber which is so often isolated from the real issues of the day. It is an unfortunate fact, but it is true. These committees should see first-hand the problems faced by the Canadians they represent.
An interesting brief was presented to the committee when they were in Fredericton, New Brunswick, by the New Brunswick Milk Producers' Association and the New Brunswick Cream Producers' Marketing Board. Among other things the brief to the Agriculture Committee states:
On March 31, 1969, the Hon. Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Olson, made this statement in the House of Commons and I quote:
"I wish to inform the house that the support price for manufacturing milk for the year commencing April 1, 1969, has been set at $4.85 per hundred pounds of milk testing 3.5 per cent butter-fat. This is the same level as that established on April 1, 1968." This price was calculated on a market price of $3.54 plus a subsidy payment of $1.31 per cwt.
I should like to point out to you gentlemen that the average price of manufacturing milk in New Brunswick last year was $3.15 not $3.54. At the present time the highest price being paid is $3.15 and it ranges to a low of $2.38. The average would be below $3.00 per cwt.
The reason for the extremely low price is the end use of the product. There is no spray powder made in New Brunswick. Due to low production and wide distances between plants there is not sufficient manufacturing milk available to support such a plant.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
A considerable amount of roller powder is produced but it sells for a lower price.
We are deficient in butter production. About 57 per cent of the butter used in New Brunswick last year was imported -from other provinces.
The phasing out policy of the Canadian Dairy Commission has contributed to our rapid decline in production. We also have a number of fluid milk and sweet cream producers who were forced out of business by the introduction of bulk tank hauling of milk. These men fall into the category of new producers when they apply for a federal quota and their only hope of obtaining one lies in their ability to purchase the herd of one who is retiring, and that must meet the requirements of 3,500 pounds butterfat for milk or 1,750 pounds in the case of a cream shipper.
The Budget-Mr. Fairweather The situation in the three Maritime provinces is much the same. Last year representatives of the three provinces held several meetings and made a presentation to the Hon. Minister of Agriculture and to the Canadian Dairy Commission. We feel that these submissions contain the substance of our requests and we therefore present them to you for consideration:
Then follows these short recommendations:
(1)	That the minimum quota for a new shipper be set at 1,750 pounds butterfat rather than the present 3.500 pounds butterfat.
(2)	That the present total quota for the Maritime provinces be retained for this region for a stated period of time. This region is deficient as far as dairy production is concerned.
(3)	That consideration should be given to a subsidy to fluid milk shippers on their surplus shipments. It was estimated that sales of subsidized spray powder in one province displaced three million dollars worth of fluid sales. If a subsidy were paid to fluid shippers on their surplus in this province, it would amount to one half million dollars. It was further pointed out that a subsidy to fluid producers on their surplus would help maintain the present fluid price to consumers.
(4) That a floor price be established for roller skim milk powder. The present floor for spray powder does not provide an automatic floor for roller powder as had been anticipated.
(5)	That the present level of phasing out smaller producers be maintained at 420 pounds butterfat.
(6)	That as the Maritime provinces do not contribute to the surplus of dairy products and as producers have several disadvantages such as higher transportation costs on milk and cream, smaller operators, higher feed costs, etc., that the holdback from the subsidy to shippers in this region be eliminated.
Out of $109,700,000 in subsidy payments in 1968, New Brunswick received $1,276,000. The total Canadian milk production used in factory products in 1968 was 11,603,62 thousand pounds. New Brunswick's share of this was a mere 115,465 thousand pounds. Total production of skim milk powder in 1968 was about 356 million pounds. New Brunswick produced a little over 2 million.
(7)	That if these recommendations cannot be implemented under the present framework of the Canadian Dairy Commission, that a special regional policy be requested for the Maritime provinces.
Once more, Mr. Speaker, I make no apology for this pleading with respect to the problems faced by a specific area of Canada. These are very real problems that have been studied backwards and forwards throughout the decades. I would hope that the government will make up its mind soon on a sensible plan of action.
The third point I wish to make in the few minutes that are available to me concerns the need for a flexible policy for bank loans. In its budget proposals the government has indicated a welcome flexibility in its approach toward the problem of inflation. I have no intention of getting into the specifics as to
1000S
June 11, 1969

The Budget-Mr. Fairweather whether Edmonton, Calgary, Toronto and other cities are over-heated from the point of view of inflation. People with greater technical ability than I possess can deal with that. But there has been a final breakthrough, after all the years of pleading, particularly by the Premiers of the Atlantic provinces, for this flexibility in approach.
I would hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), would add to this flexibility something of what is done in the federal reserve system in the United States whereby in a period of high interest rates and tight money, such as we are again entering, directions can be readily given, without the need for any legislation, to the lending institutions of the country whereby regions where economic disparity is evident will have bank financing available to them. This can be done by the minister with the stroke of a pen, and I would hope he would see fit to carry out this proposal.
There is no need, and the budget has indicated this, to attack the problems of the country in totality, in a total centralized policy. We need flexibility if we are really to do something toward bringing those regions of the country that have not enjoyed the advantage of what I might call full citizenship up to the standards of other parts of the country, so that the citizens of the part of the country that I represent may take their place in a buoyant economy.
The last matter I wish to speak upon, and as in all speeches just because it is the last this does not mean I consider it less important than the others, is pollution. I think it is high time the government co-ordinated their efforts in their attack upon pollution. We have had a most interesting constitutional minuet from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), ever since he assumed office, about the problem of pollution control. We have had various ministers who have varying degrees of responsibility for this great national and international problem.
We have had first rate speeches from the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) who assures us that under the Fisheries Act he has the competence and the power to deal with this problem. We have had word from the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) that very soon he will introduce a new water act. We also used to have statements about pollution from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Greene).
Until this government, the provinces and the municipalities are able to agree on a formula to fight pollution and are able to agree that a corporation guilty of pollution should be liable, just as a citizen is liable for damaging another's property or person, we will really not have faced this issue at all. The Minister of Fisheries-I do not think this is a disclosure of something private, but if so I apologize, although I guess, it is readily available information-told me that in most construction of pulp mills adequate pollution controls would cost less than 2 per cent of the capital needed for the construction. I think this is another issue upon which the government is a light year behind the public of Canada in really facing up to the need for adequate measures to ensure that the people of Canada have clean water, clean land and clean air. These are the points that have been concerning me for some time, Mr. Speaker, and I thank members of the house for their attention.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) since he assumed that office less than a year ago. It has become a practice for Liberal ministers of finance to introduce two budgets a year. I assume this is on the principle that the second budget is designed to offset the errors and the omissions of the first budget. This particular budget which the minister has announced with a great blare of trumpets is to begin the battle against inflation. Well, if some of us are not impressed by this call to battle it is because we remember that four years ago, with great tooting of trumpets and unfurling of flags, a Liberal government was out to wage war on poverty. It will be recalled that that war came to an end without ever a shot being fired. The best proof that the government did not even engage in the war is the last annual review of the Economic Council of Canada which found that between 20 per cent and 25 per cent of the people of this country were living below the poverty line.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The minister is to wage war against inflation. All of us, of course, would like to wish him well but I submit that all he has produced so far has been two wooden swords, neither of which are likely to slay the dragon of inflation. As a matter of fact, before he even begins the battle the minister admits his estimate for the coming year is that the cost of living will rise by some 4 per cent. That is

June 11. 1969	COMMONS
what it rose last year and is approximately what it rose the year before. So, even before he begins to tackle inflation the minister has already told us we can expect a situation no better, and many of us suspect it will be somewhat worse, than what it has been in the past year. As a matter of fact all the indicators suggest there will probably be an increase in the cost of living as high as 4.7 per cent.
The minister has suggested two things which he proposes to do to cope with inflation. They are commendable moves, but neither of them really grapples with the problem. The first suggestion is that there is to be a two-year deferment on depreciation of capital costs for Commercial Construction, in cities which have a population of over 50,000 people in the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta. The idea of selective investment allocation is good. We in this party have been suggesting some type of selective program and the establishment of priorities for a long time. I would point out, however, that this proposal is not likely to be very effective and will not do the thing the minister hopes it will do. Corporations intending to erect commercial buildings, in anticipation of an increase in construction costs, in all likelihood will decide that the increased cost of buildings two years from now could be greater than the cost to them of foregoing the capital depreciation for a period of two years. Even if this should have some effect on construction programs in certain areas, there is no guarantee whatsoever that these funds will automatically be transferred either to low cost housing or to the underdeveloped areas in Canada.
The minister's second proposal is to implement the recommendations of the Kennedy round immediately rather than spread them over the two and a half years they have to run. Again, no one can object to this. I would point out that the reductions are minor; that most of the reductions are 3 per cent or less; that a large number of the items affected are producer or intermediary goods, and that there is no guarantee whatsoever that the savings effected will be passed on to the consumer. Certainly, if we look at the Canada-United States auto agreement under which this parliament gave to the automobile manufacturers some $50 million a year in the form of duty which they no longer had to pay, on the assumption that this would have the effect of reducing the price of cars to the Canadian consumer, we can see that the savings have not been passed on and that the disparity
The Budget-Mr. T. C. Douglas between the price of cars in Canada and in the United States remains roughly the same.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is failing to come to grips with the basic problems in this country. Do we have inflation? The common definition of inflation is too much money chasing too few goods. Is there too much money? Certainly, in certain quarters there is a great deal of money. Certain areas of the economy have done very well and have made large profits. Capital gains have been made on the stock market and on land speculation. But is there too much money in the pockets of the veterans of this country who have been waiting for years to get an increase in the war veterans' allowance and who have been promised for years that when the Woods report came down they would be looked after? Now, when the report has come down they are told they will have to wait for a white paper. No doubt when the white paper comes in they will be told they must wait for the report of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. These peter-ans have less money in terms of spending power than they had five years ago.
What about the people on fixed incomes? Have they too much money? They have less money in real terms than they had five years ago. The old age pensioners find that the cost of living went up last year 4 per cent but the government provides only for a 2 per cent increase in their cost of living bonus. In addition, if they are under the age of 70 and receive the supplementary allowance they will pay income tax. This will mean that in effect they will be giving back the 2 per cent cost of living bonus they receive. They do not have too much money. They are worse off than they were before this government took office. Are the four million or five million people in Canada who live below the poverty line suffering from too much money? Are the 400,000 or 450,000 unemployed overburdened with a supply of money? Are the farmers of this country suffering from too much money, particularly the western farmers who have millions of bushels of wheat stored on their farms but who are unable to obtain sufficient cash to meet their obligations? Certainly, there is not too much money there.
I know of course that these are the vested interests the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has promised to bring to heel in order to cure inflation. This government has failed to face the fact that the problem is not too much money. The problem in this country is a maldistribution of income and misallocation of
10008	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. T. C. Douglas
the available resources of Canada. The fact is that the government, ever since it took office in 1963, has consistently increased the tax burden on the low and middle income groups but has continued special privileges for the wealthy in this country.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
The personal income tax has been raised repeatedly while corporation taxes have been treated with kid gloves. There was an increase in corporation taxes by 5 per cent refundable tax imposed in March, 1966. I underline the words "refundable tax" because these corporations were to get their payments back in 18 months at 5J per cent interest. The wage and salary earners are not going to get their tax payments back, interest or no interest. Even then, the refundable tax was cancelled in 1967.
Then the government found, of course, it had to repay the tax it collected, plus the interest. It had to find $244 million. Early in 1968 the government endeavoured to put through this house a 5 per cent surcharge on the wage and salary earners in order to get enough money to repay this corporation refundable tax. Fortunately, that move was stopped by the combined opposition Parties of parliament.
Then, the government compromised and brought in a surcharge of 3 per cent on both personal and corporate income tax. That was supposed to expire at the end of this calendar year, 1969. Under this budget it is going to be extended to the end of 1970. In that year the 3 percent tax is going to bring in $150 million, $40 million of which will be corporate taxes and $110 million personal income taxes.
Not satisfied with this discrimination in fiscal inequity, the government is now introducing a social development tax of 2 per cent which is levied solely on the wage and salary earners. It is not to be paid by corporations. To make matters even worse, it applies only to the first $6,000 of taxable income, so people with $40,000 or $50,000 per year are to pay the same tax as somebody earning $8,000 or $10,000 per year.
When the Prime Minister told the national convention of chambers of commerce that the rich were overtaxed, I wonder what he had in mind about the poor and the people in the middle and lower income groups whose taxes have been going up steadily? This country is suffering from maldistribution of income; some have too much but many have too little. The government has completely ignored the

DEBATES	June 11, 1969
recommendations of the Carter commission. The government has been promising us a white paper for over a year.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is coming.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is coming, but when is some action coming? The government could apply a tax on the banks. This morning's Globe and Mail states that in the six months ending April 30 the seven chartered banks have made an average increase of 33 per cent on their profits, and their stocks have gone sky high ever since the ceiling was taken off interest rates. The oil and mining companies could be made to pay taxes on the same basis as other corporations.
I remember when the Minister of Finance sat over here in 1962 and excoriated the government of that day for not removing some of the depletion and depreciation allowances enjoyed by the mining and oil industries. What is he doing about that now? What about recognizing the facts of the capital gains tax so that those who make profits out of the stock exchange or speculation on land development will be required to treat their profits as income and pay taxes the same as anyone else?
The government does not need a white paper. It has all the data it needs and it has the information contained in the Carter report. What the government lacks is backbone. I could make a better backbone out of a banana than the backbone possessed by this government. The government could collect taxes from those who are the freeloaders in our economy. The government could still, after that, reduce personal income tax for people with incomes of $10,000 per year or less by 15 per cent and have more revenue that it has now.
The government has not only failed to do anything about the redistribution of income, it has failed to do anything about social and economic priorities. It removed the ceiling on bank rates without any safeguards. We are paying the price of that now. It introduced legislation to increase the capitalization of trust and loan companies, granting them greater access to money markets. It has a tax system which encourages equity investment rather than bond investment. The result is an absurd imbalance in our priorities.
The private sector is able to get capital, but the public sector is hard pressed in respect of schools, hospitals, urban renewal projects, low cost housing and recreational facilities.
June 11. 1969

These are just as important as having another filling station on the corner or a third supermarket in each subdivision.
This government's fiscal policy over the years has starved the public sector. It is amazing that in a society which needs hospitals, schools and the social amenities, when times are good we cannot have these amenities because of inflation and when times are bad we cannot have them because we cannot afford them. The government asks where we would get the money. If financial resources are scarce, this is all the more reason to space out private investment in less productive areas of the economy and concentrate on those things which will increase productivity.
One of the things of which the government is guilty is that it has failed to put a major emphasis on stepping up economic growth. If, as the Minister of Finance says, there is too much money in relation to goods, surely the thing to do is put the emphasis on increasing the amount of goods.
Unemployment represents a loss of potential production. Having between 400,000 and 450,000 unemployed, we have a shortfall in our production in this country of $3 billion to $4 billion. In Europe they have been placing the emphasis on full employment, so that in countries like West Germany and Sweden they have unemployment down to 1 or 11 per cent.
In this country unemployment has been the means the government has used to cool off the economy. The former Minister of Finance very callously said it might be necessary to have some slack in the economy. We have been getting slack in the economy by deliberately fomenting unemployment. The strange thing is that in a classical economy it has always been understood that if you have a period of inflation you have a danger of rising prices but full employment, but in a period of deflation you have unemployment and falling prices. Only a government of geniuses could get the worst of both worlds in which we have both rising prices and unemployment.
This government gives no indication in this budget that its fiscal and monetary policies are designed to stimulate productivity or to provide for full employment as one of the best means to combat inflation. The Minister of Finance is very proud of the fact that he has balanced his budget. I want to suggest that he is balancing it on the hardships and the heartaches of the most defenceless segment of our society. The government's idea of combatting inflation by cutting government 29180-633
The Budget-Mr. Perrault spending is reminiscent of the economics of Herbert Hoover.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Government spending is not wasteful spending if it is properly administered. Much of government spending represents a distribution of income; it represents taxing those who have the ability to pay, and providing through pensions and other measures income for those who live below the poverty line. One of the greatest omissions in this budget, may I say in conclusion, is the fact that there is not any indication at all that the government is aware of the disastrous situation which obtains in the three prairie provinces of Canada where farmers, because of declining prices, reduced deliveries and a catastrophic drop in wheat sales, face the most serious situation that I have seen on the prairies since the 1930's. There is not a line in the budget that indicates the government is prepared to spend a dollar to meet that situation.
For three months now we have listened to ministers saying the matter is under consideration. The government's policy will be made known in due course, says each minister, like a puppet on the end of a string. But the Minister of Finance has given us no indication whatsoever that the government has any policy; that it intends to make any money available so that the farmers of western Canada will be able to get sufficient cash income to buy their supplies for summer fallowing, for their weed-spraying, and for harvesting a crop this fall, to say nothing of the money they will need to provide for their families. It would appear that this government is prepared to let western agriculture go down the drain. We in this party will have more to say about that matter unless the government indicates fairly soon that it has a program and a policy by which it will put cash into the hands of the farmers of western Canada.
Therefore, because this budget will do little or nothing to combat the present inflationary situation, and because it is replete with social injustice, we members of the New Democratic party will vote for the amendment and against the budget.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the presentation which we have just heard, I wonder whether the research grants made available to party leaders have been properly spent. We have
10010	COMMONS DEBATES	June 11. 1969
The Budget-Mr. Perrault just heard a catalogue of inaccuracies, perhaps unintentional, and a recitation of misinterpretation which I shall attempt, at least in part, to correct. Before I do, I would like to make the general observation that in recent days we have heard the usual round of budget criticism which we have come to expect from some members of the opposition. Unfailingly, these critics shroud their comments in gloom and doom. There is not one qualified word of support for any aspect of the budget. They condemn it. Indeed, during the past session some of these spokesmen-and some are leading members of the house-have been so loath to approve anything the government has done that their words of approval have been as rare as the dodo bird or the passenger pigeon. But in this particular debate, in the context of the economic problem facing Canada, there is an unreal quality about the unrestrained assault upon the budget.
Opposition spokesmen-and I suggest it is an old fashioned political technique-seem compelled to act out the charade of attacking a budget in all its aspects; pointing with alarm; suggesting that people are being ground down into poverty, and resurrecting all the old cliches which we identify with the class struggle of the 1930's. The response is a negative stereotype. It does not do the opposition very much good. People want to know what the opposition parties have to offer as alternatives. I began to write down some of the alternatives I have heard in this house during the past few days, and I do not have even half a sheet of constructive comments from opposition spokesmen. Yet they aspire to forming the government of Canada.
Let us examine some of the myths. Myth No. 1 is this: The opposition claims that this government is clinging desperately to an outmoded system of taxation; that it resists change and reform. This is one of the most nonsensical myths of all. The existing taxation system is going to be changed, and the opposition knows it. It is to be hoped that the opposition parties will participate in assisting that change with a few rare, constructive proposals. A white paper containing a draft of taxation changes will be released in the near future. It will undoubtedly contain some of the recommendations of the Carter Commission report which will dismay some of our friends in the New Democratic party opposition.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why wait till spring; do it now.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
These recommendations will be considered by the government and other people across the country, including labour unions, businessmen, management and banking people. The Carter Commission report, like all reports of its kind, is not binding on the government; no royal commission report ever was. Certainly, such reports were not binding when my hon. friend was premier of Saskatchewan; he developed his own policy. Revised methods of raising revenue will be adopted, subject to amendments, but only after nation-wide examination and discussion of the white paper proposals.
No one disagrees with the statement of the hon. member who just spoke, namely, that we have to bring a greater degree of equity and fairness to the taxation system in Canada. Government members would like to see exemptions increased, more money for senior citizens, and all the rest. But the suggestion that somehow government benches are occupied by hard-hearted Simon Legrees, determined to provide more and more difficulties for senior citizens and those on fixed incomes, is simply untrue.
The official opposition spokesman, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), who is a very articulate member, was unremitting in his attack. I would remind the official opposition that they had six long years to bring about greater justice and equity in the taxation system of Canada. They showed all the enterprise of a sloth in effecting really meaningful reform. All they succeeded in doing was tinkering with the machinery. I am pleased that we have a government which questions whether in the Canada of 1969 we need brand new machinery.
As far as the minor opposition parties are concerned, the New Democratic party, when entrusted with the responsibility of governing Saskatchewan, did nothing to reform the basic relationship between the municipalities and the provincial government-nothing except to impose over 200 new taxes, imposts, fees and other charges against the long-suffering public. The result was that 200,000 people left Saskatchewan during those balmy years to seek opportunity elsewhere, the largest exodus since Moses led his people into the promised land.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I recall the monumental statement of the Creditiste leader when he was in Vancouver several days ago. He told an audience in that city that the Creditiste

June 11. 1969

party had a simple solution to all the problems; they would abolish all debt in Canada with the stroke of a pen. This should strike terror into the heart of any responsible Canadian.
Myth No. 2 is that a profligate, intemperate government is investing millions of dollars in unrewarding programs of social development, and that waste is rampant. These are the words that have been used. The federal government has increased its spending; but where has it gone? These are the facts which have not been cited by the leader of the New Democratic party and others who have participated in this debate. I tell this house that combined provincial-municipal expenditures have grown from less than half of federal spending in the early 1950's to more than the total of federal expenditures. The provincial use of major tax fields has grown correspondingly. All provinces now receive one quarter of the personal income taxes paid and Quebec receives an additional 23 per cent under the contracting-out arrangements. The ten provinces receive almost one quarter of corporation income tax, almost 40 per cent of all commodity taxes, and virtually all natural resource levies. Yet there is a suggestion that the federal government is somehow taking in all this money and that it is not being effectively spent. All the provinces have benefited from federal payments on tax abatements, so much so that in the last seven years the amount of these payments has risen from $898 million to an estimated $2,811 million.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Where has this money gone? We have heard a lot about this unsympathetic government which does not want to help the low income groups. Here are some figures which hon. members might bear in mind. Medicare, $325 million; fiscal transfers to provinces, $100.8 million; hospital insurance, $65 million; post-secondary education, $53 million; Canada assistance plan, $48.4 million, for a total of $602.2 million.
Then, there is the cost of the regional economic expansion program, $45.9 million; grants for urban renewal, sewage treatment and housing research, $10.9 million, and the Cape Breton Development Corporation, $3 million, a total of $59.8 million, representing in all a total increase in the estimates of $1,031.7 million. These funds were spent on services destined primarily to assist low income groups and the less privileged parts of our society. Yet the house has been inflicted
10011
The Budget-Mr. Perrault with statements along the lines that this government is a government which does not care. We heard the official opposition attacking the government the other day for what was alleged to be flagrant misspending. Opposition spokesmen said spending exceeded all understandable limits. Mr. Speaker, I intend to quote a former prime minister of Canada, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), speaking in a notable debate which took place on June 27, 1961:
Is it wasteful to spend more money to fight recession? Is it wasteful to bring social assistance to additional Canadians? Is it wasteful to provide more funds for the provinces and municipalities? Is it wasteful to spend money to further national development? These are some of the kinds of expenditures that were made, all of which were necessary to meet a situation.
The official opposition has absolutely no compunction about complaining that the government is wasting money. Yet, when they were themselves in power their leader stated that when money was well spent its outlay was fully justified. This is the kind of argument which has been used to condemn the budget out of hand. Those who say money is being wasted should bear in mind the fact that the total federal contribution to the provinces as a percentage of total federal budgetary expenditures less tax rental payments grew from 14.46 per cent in 1961-62 to 26.08 per cent in 1968-69.
This government has had the courage to question some of the existing programs and to initiate co-operative studies with the provinces to make certain that social development dollars are being expended as usefully as possible. This is what should be done. The government stated-and I hope no hon. member disagrees with this-on the subject of social welfare:
A general intergovernmental agreement on the three programs is also proposed under which: (a) all governments would agree to continue joint consultations to discuss operation and improvement of the programs, (b) the federal government would agree to provide technical assistance to improve program standards, and (c) the provinces would agree to maintain uniform residence rules to ensure interprovincial portability of hospital and welfare benefits to individuals.
Then there is the demand that some specific monetary and fiscal measures be applied to counter the effects of inflation. Mr. Speaker, the problem we face today is the concern of the entire world. Statistics have been cited in connection with Sweden. I should like to answer some of the questions which have been raised in this house about Sweden.

one of the most fallacious arguments of all. The party that advanced this concept of lower interest rates announced dramatically one Monday morning that that same party professed to concern itself with the plight of the less fortunate. Yet such action by Canada would result in widespread ruin, first of all among those who are forced to eke out an existence on fixed incomes.
The official opposition have offered criticisms based on today's inflationary situation. I would remind them of the speech made by their own minister of finance when they were in power in 1960. As reported at page 2672 of Hansard for March 31, 1960, he said:
We must place emphasis on greater productivity and efficiency rather than on sheer size-
He called for the co-operation of all sectors of the community. He said that the government could not solve the problem by itself and, of course, he was correct. He stated that the role of leadership falls to the federal government; that it is the responsibility of the government to try to establish conditions of financial balance. I suggest that this is not within the control of this government or any other single government. We must remember that municipal governments and provincial governments in Canada are now spending more than the federal government. Consequently, unless they act responsibly, and unless labour and management act responsibly, we cannot control inflation. The federal government could reduce its budget by 50 per cent,, but we still might not be able to attain our objective.
In conclusion-
