subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to participate in the budget debate. The budget speech proposes to deal with inflation. In fact, the news release by the minister under the title "Budget Highlights" states that the No. 1 priority in economic policy today is to deploy all available forces, public and private, more aggressively than ever in the battle against inflation.
The minister speaks about inflation as though it were a recent occurrence, as though he and his party only recently became shipmates with this phenomenon which is eroding the purchasing power of our dollar like the worms erode the planks in the bottom of a ship. Just as the worm holes in the planking eventually cause the ship to sink, inflation is taking its terrible toll on the economy of our Canadian ship of state.
If we want to know when inflation started running rampant, like a malignant cancer, through our economy, all we have to do is to read the minister's economic white paper for 1969. His very first statement is a tribute to the previous Conservative administration, for the minister states that in early 1969 the Canadian economy entered its ninth year of expansion. It is gratifying to see a Liberal admit, even at this late date, that the Canadian economy was expanding in 1960.
The minister went on to say, according to the white paper:
Since 1965, increases in prices have been larger than desirable, and public policy has been designed to replace inflationary expansion by balanced and sustained growth.
Which public policies is the minister referring to at this time? Is he referring to the 60 days of decision, or to the bankrupt policies of Mr. Walter Gordon, whose budgets were a mish-mash of proposals which were inflationary and many of which had to be withdrawn? Is the minister referring to the establishment of the ill-fated industry department, which increased all government costs by raiding departments by inflated salary offers that caused demands from all departments for increased wages. Eventually, the industry department had to be put back where it belonged with trade and commerce? Was this one of the Liberal government's anti-inflationary policies? Are these people trying to suggest to us that this juggling of departments served to save us money? Or perhaps the

June 11, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Crouse finance minister is referring to the Canada Pension Plan, which this government made compulsory even though thousands of Canadians asked that it be made voluntary? Its implementation required hundreds of additional staff, adding to the taxpayers' load and to inflation in Canada.
Or was the finance minister referring to Mr. Pearson's 30 per cent settlement formula when he spoke of policies designed to replace inflationary expansion? By granting this enormous pay raise when settling the strike on June 14,	1966,, almost three years ago,
between the International Longshoremen's Association in Montreal and the Shipping Federation of Canada, the Liberal party set the standard, the target, for all wage demands in this country.
Or perhaps the finance minister was referring to medicare when he spoke of policies designed to curb inflation. Here we have a policy that even wealthy Ontario and Quebec still question because of its cost and inflationary effect on their economies, while poor New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island must pay their share though lacking the further resources required to provide this service to their people.
The unfavourable situation that led to rising inflation is in the main due to the lack of forward planning by the Liberal government for most of its shared cost programs. Here I refer to post-secondary education and the Canada assistance plan, in addition to the other programs I have already mentioned. The inevitable result of these policies is that our financial system has now got out of control.
The minister cannot have it both ways. He claims the establishment of a sound economic and financial base on the one hand, while saying on the other hand that inflation really became a problem in 1965. I ask him and his government: Why did the Liberal party, which has been in power since 1963, do nothing to curb inflation in the past six years? Bather it brought in policies that made the inflationary fires burn brighter and higher. There is really no excuse for the mismanagement of our affairs by the Liberal government. There is no excuse for their arrogance or for their indifference. The fact that successive Liberal administrations have refused to take action on inflationary problems has destroyed the government's credibility.
We now see the minister further destroying his own credibility by piously stating that this

government's No. 1 priority in economic policy must be to deploy all public and private forces more aggressively than ever in the battle against inflation. Of course this should be the government's No. 1 priority, but indifference on the part of many Canadians to the minister's budget proposals indicates that nobody believes him any longer. That is both his and his government's real problem-that nobody believes them any longer.
What does this budget do for Atlantic Canada? To date Liberal policies have done very little for our area. The government's lack of a shipbuilding policy has brought our shipbuilders close to the brink of financial ruin. In the Atlantic provinces today there are, according to chart 9 on page 25 of the minister's white paper, some 50,000 men without jobs. This represents more than 10 per cent of the labour force. Were this level of unemployment prevalent all across the country, the cabinet would, react as if faced with a national disaster-and rightly so. Put in other terms, the unemployment rate in the Atlantic provinces is half again as high as it is in Canada as a whole.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The Atlantic provinces have other characteristics, Mr. Speaker. The employed worker in Atlantic Canada is paid, on the average, only 82 per cent of the amount the average Canadian receives. We all know that capital growth in the Atlantic region is slower than in the rest of Canada. Not only is it generally lower, but it is subject to boom and bust fluctuations. The minister tells us that the 1969 outlook in the Atlantic provinces is still mixed. This problem, of course, is well known to everyone who has studied problems of regional growth. However, what we should like to see is a steady and continuing expansion so that the best use is made of our resources, physical and human, for the benefit of the region and the country as a whole. For example, we need legislation to deal with our pollution problems; we need adequate legislation to introduce regulations to deal with our fisheries resources.
What has been offered by the Liberal party, Mr. Speaker? In the first place, the government has given us rapid inflation, and with that inflation has come all the dislocation inflation can cause. We have had few of the benefits that accrue to some groups and regions during periods of rapid price increase. Few of those benefits have come to the Atlantic region. On previous occasions I have brought the dimensions of inflation to the
June 11. 1969

attention of the treasury benches. A dollar earned in 1961 has a purchasing power today of approximately 75 cents; and the sad but true fact is that the 75 cent dollar of today will be worth only 60 cents one year from now if the April rate of deterioration continues for 12 months.
Inflation lays a heavy hand on those who are working; but it is a nightmare to some of our senior citizens and pensioners. The victims of inflation are easy to identify, if any one cares to look. They are welfare cases, the hard core unemployed, the old age pensioners, the widows and orphans living on fixed incomes and the voiceless, unorganized workers in our society. To this group will be added the wage earners who will eventually be laid off as inflation erodes what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has called the competitive position of Canadian producers in those other countries with which we must trade and in our own markets at home. The immediate removal of the three remaining stages of the Kennedy round of tariff reductions is designed to increase price competition. In my view that will only be done at the expense of increased unemployment in Canada.
When the government forms policies to fight inflation there is always the danger that the problems of regional disparity which I outlined earlier will be aggravated. In the words of the budget papers, these regional differences add to the problems of designing a policy for stabilization and growth.
On Tuesday night last we noted that the minister made some attempt to meet this problem in one field of activity by deferring for two years cost allowances on commercial buildings specifically in British Columbia, Ontario and Alberta. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, this policy contradicts directly the Prime Minister's election promise of equal treatment for all provinces. This type of policy brought forward by the Liberal party does not jibe with promises made during the federal election campaign. The Liberal party, in fighting that campaign, said that its policies were designed to unite Canada. I can think of no comparable policy which will place a greater strain on confederation. But it is not realistic to dwell on this one measure when the most important aspects of the budget dealing with traditional monetary and fiscal policies apply to areas of slow economic growth with the magnified effect that such aspects have always had on such areas.
The Budget-Mr. Crouse
Canada as a whole has been denied the sensible, interim policies advocated by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). I refer here, of course, to his proposition that a flexible, short term policy of well known and nationally acceptable economic guidelines, especially with regard to prices and wages, be instituted in addition to other policies to see us through the present inflationary crisis. The deficiencies of guidelines we all recognize. Nevertheless, we prefer the lesser deficiencies of temporary guidelines to the long term harm which inflation and ill fitting economic policies can wreak in whole regions of Canada and among whole income groups.
Generally speaking, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has undertaken to keep government spending constant. This is in line with the recommendations of the economic council and the opinions of many economists who have been dismayed at the almost rampant growth of expenditure by government these last four or five years. There has been great dismay with regard to the wasteful extravagance of government. I submit that keeping the lid on the budget is not enough. Changing needs or the existence of old needs which have not yet been met require a constant reappraisal by government of its priorities. The government should turn its attention to the priority of building an infrastructure. Within this general priority, precedence should be given to projects which meet the real needs of the people of the country. The National Arts Centre which cost $46 million represents, I think it is fair to say, too great a portion of our nation's resources being applied to the non-urgent needs of too few people. There are thousands of smaller projects costing tens of thousands of dollars-not tens of millions-which meet today's bread and. butter needs. In most cases these projects have what could be termed a multiplier effect. These projects do not need government subsidies to make sure that full use is made of them. Instead, these projects will stimulate economic activity and enable human and physical resources, formerly lying unused or partially used, to be applied productively.
I cannot understand, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure many Canadians cannot understand, the government's sense of priorities. On Thursday, May 29, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) outlined the government's plans for the national capital region, indicating the government's intention to develop Hull into a major government employment centre. Now, I do not object to

June 11, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Crouse the incorporation of the City of Hull in the national capital area; neither do I object to the idea of extending and beautifying the national capital region, within reason, through the expenditure of public money. That idea I think is acceptable to most Canadians. This government, however, must soon make up its mind as to what it wants to do. It cannot continue in its hypocritical way; it cannot continue saying one thing and doing another. It cannot talk about practising economies, instituting controls and cutting back on expenditures and the number of its employees on the one hand while throwing away all common sense and restraint on the other hand, and still remain credible. The rate at which Canada Savings Bonds are being cashed indicates that this government's credibility already is at a low ebb. All the Minister of Finance can do in responding to this situation is to get out the whip and let it cut a little deeper into the backbone of Canadians by extending the existing surtax on personal and corporate income until the end of 1970. What arrogance is this, Mr. Speaker? What gall.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion has told us that there will be accommodation for about 36,000 public service employees in Hull. At this very moment the National Capital Commission is filing expropriation documents, because the initial requirement for making the development possible is land for building sites. In the light of this announcement, surely the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the entire cabinet will not continue with their hypocrisy surely they will not continue with this charade and try to tell us they are practising economy in government. Quite obviously the men sitting on the treasury benches do not know the meaning of the word "economy". I am beginning to wonder whether any of them has actually worked for a dollar. They do not understand its value, and the value of our dollar is getting less and less every year.
I say that this government is false to its trust in administering public funds. While they are going to great extremes to acquire through expropriation land for public buildings in Hull, there are at present seven temporary buildings in Ottawa which could be torn down for one tenth of the cost of the land in Hull. The buildings required for government administration could be built on the land occupied by these temporary buildings. Whereas these existing buildings are only two 
stories high, their replacements could contain sufficient stories to house adequately existing and expanding government departments for some time. That, Mr. Speaker, would be the common sense approach. Unfortunately common sense is one ingredient that is sadly lacking in this administration.
We have here a government that admits, for example, that a skidway is required by the 38 fishermen of lower Jordan Bay in Shelburne county. They operate 28 boats there. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) concurred in the recommendation that this much needed facility be built. That happened away back on December 5, 1968, but because of lack of funds the work has not been started. The cost of this much needed facility would be under $10,000 and would aid these primary producers in earning a living from the sea. However, it cannot be developed because of lack of funds, yet the government talks of millions for the national capital area.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Similarly, in the town of Bridgewater, a new federal building is required. Two years ago this was approved by the then Minister of Public Works. To date this government has been unable to find a suitable site or indicate when construction will be started. In the town of Liverpool this government assisted in the development of a floating fish plant. There are thousands of dollars in federal funds tied up in that plant, but now silt has filled in Liverpool Harbour and it requires dredging. At low tide the edge of that plant is aground which is causing it to get out of shape and impedes the operation of that particular plant. We have done everything but provide funds for dredging. The government says, sorry old boy, we have nothing for you. There are funds for the wealthy areas of Canada which set the living standards for the nation, while there are not even any crumbs for those areas still suffering from regional disparity.
If the minister wants to re-establish faith in Canada and in Canadian securities, a relatively simple procedure is open to him. Let him change the income tax laws. Instead of allowing a 20 per cent deduction for dividends received from taxable Canadian companies, I suggest for a start that he raise this amount to 40 per cent. I am sure the minister will be pleasantly surprised at how quickly Canadian securities will be found more attractive than United States securities for Canadian capital, while the loss to the treasury will be minimal.
June 11, 1969

I firmly believe we must encourage thrift in this country and reward initiative and ambition if we really want to develop Canada. Unless we get greater Canadian participation in our resource development, we will not have the means to sustain our economic growth at its present level and we will not have the means to control this malignant cancer which we call inflation.

speechtext:
I was not suggesting that, Mr. Speaker. I was suggesting he did not mention rental expenditures and it would have put things in their proper perspective if they had been mentioned.
I follow two other distinguished members from the area which I represent, the hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens) and the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Weatherhead), who spoke on the two previous days of this debate. I support the remarks they made. We represent an area of this country which is blessed, the area of greater Metropolitan Toronto. This area is blessed in very many ways, yet we have many concerns and many legitimate needs. Not all of our people are so blessed. We do have problems.
While we certainly represent our constituents to the best of our ability and with all the energy we have, we realize, as do our constituents and the vast majority of people in that part of the country, that our major concerns are for a united country and a stable
The Budget-Mr. Danson economy. We are determined to put forward our demands on behalf of the legitimate interests of our area, but never at the expense of national interest. So often when speaking of Toronto, people use funny names. I think that is a part of history that has been forgotten.
I do not need to apologize for the city of Toronto. I am proud to be from that area and proud of my city. As the hon. member for York West has pointed out, approximately one-third of the personal tax, corporation tax and sales tax comes from that area. That is because we are part of Canada, and that is the way we should keep it. There is a suggestion we are not getting our fair share. While there are many things for which we wish, we must keep our needs in perspective. Perhaps our needs, priorities and even our values in some respects in our area are different from those required or wanted by others.
In the area of national housing expenditures, public housing and student housing, the greater Metropolitan area of Toronto between the years 1963 and 1967 received over $1 billion. That is double what any other city of any size in Canada has received. Our Museum of Science and Technology, a provincial centennial project, received $2.5 million from the federal government. The St. Lawrence Centre for the Arts received $665,000. The Toronto District Conservation Authority has received grants totalling up to $9 million. There are some questions in relation to the repayment of some of these funds, $1,200,000. The members from our area are working diligently to get a fair appropriation for the type of public facility that is not only vital to the safety of the people in that community, in view of the tragedy of Hurricane Hazel some years ago, but which will also provide recreation areas and flood control.
There have been approximately $54 million in municipal development loans over the years, including some loans which were not repayable for the great subway which exists in our city. Manpower, occupational and language training, which are vital in a great municipality such as ours, are of particular concern because most of the immigrants that come to this country come to our city. We welcome them and hope many more will come. Between the years 1966 and 1969, $154 million has been received for those purposes. That is money well spent.
We require better airport facilities that are consistent with the size and needs of our community, for both the international and domestic flights that pour into our area.
10018	COMMONS DEBATES	June 11, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Danson [DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
When members of parliament from the Toronto area come to Ottawa, writers in our local newspapers often criticize us. One accused us of becoming statesmen. I think that was meant as an insult; however, I take it as a compliment, although it is totally inaccurate. We are concerned, and rightly so, with the totality of our nation. The Toronto area members are working diligently to represent their area, but not at the expense of the rest of the country. I am proud to serve with men of this calibre, who think in those terms and who are prepared to back up their words with energy and work on behalf of the area they represent. Above all, we from our area are grateful for our prosperity, although it is not universal throughout our area. But we realize this prosperity will be short-lived if the value of our dollar continues to diminish and other areas of the country are not also prosperous.
Living in the biggest city in the world is not the same thing as living in the best city. We want to see a city rich in its culture, exciting in its diversity, and wholesome in its quality. To force feed a city with the chamber of commerce approach, bigness for the sake of bigness, does not interest me. I do not think it interests my colleagues. We want the things that are good in life. We have a viable community now, and it will grow of its own volition, even more so than we want. We are now waking up to the problems of living in a big city. It is living in a fool's paradise-and Toronto is no fool's paradise-to think that we can be isolated from the problems of other less prosperous areas.
It was rather interesting listening to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), that is, the Leader of the Loyal Opposition, or the Official Leader-as a matter of fact I get quite confused as to who is the leader over there, but that is because it is pretty confusing over there.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition said that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) had not been satisfied with the October budget. This is a valid observation. If he had 
been satisfied with it he would not have found the need for even stronger measures. The Leader of the Opposition said that the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment were not acceptable. Inflation and unemployment are never acceptable, but in developing budgets there is a rather delicate sort of balance to be struck. You have to try and find the proper level at which you can achieve the maximum results in restraining inflation and keeping unemployment to a minimum.
In a way it is rather sad to hear these criticisms but no alternatives. It is simple to criticize when one does not have responsibility. But I think it is a most imaginative budget. It is unique in its way, and really to see the affects it might have we have to put it in balance. The hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Perrault) pointed this out very well.
As I understand it, and I do not mean to be redundant, the Canadian position is one of which we can be really proud because inflation is not completely within our control. We are subject to international influences, but we do have some controls and we are trying to implement them. After West Germany and Italy, we are the third country in the world in ability to control the rate of the growth of inflation-not that this is good enough or is something that should make us complacent. This is not the case at all. We must keep on working at it.
In a recent letter to the constituents in my riding, I identified my own priorities in the federal government as inflation and national unity, fighting inflation and strengthening national unity. I think this budget attacks inflation, and it very much affects national unity. National unity is very much dependent upon the economic well being of our entire country.
The Atlantic provinces and Quebec are experiencing unemployment of a particular severity, and we cannot be immune from that or insensitive to it. Some areas of the west have perennial problems which must be attacked vigorously. Those problems are now aggravated by wheat surpluses while world markets are glutted. If we want a cohesive nation we must put our money where our mouth is.
The official language bill will not solve the problems of national unity all by itself, although it is a very important measure. The measures in this budget attack regional disparity while attacking inflation. Should these measures work, even to a significant degree,
June 11, 1969

it could go down as one of the most brilliant budgets in the history of our country. There are no guarantees. There are no sure formulae. But there is a delicate balance, and the budget is imaginative. I think we could be criticized if we did nothing. The fact that we are doing things that are good and imaginative, trying to pinpoint the problems, is to the credit of the Minister of Finance. I have yet to hear of more workable solutions from hon. members opposite.
Really, Mr. Speaker, all is not gloom and doom. Our gross national product for the coming year is predicted to increase at a rate of 9 per cent. It is true that 4 per cent of this will be attributable to inflation, but our net gain, in gross national product will be 5 per cent. That is not bad. In the past 12 months unemployment has declined, but it is still too severe in many areas. In other areas, like my own and the 21 other communities affected by the deferment in the tax write-offs on nonproductive construction, the strength of the economic expansion continues to aggravate the serious inflationary pressures. Construction is up 8.3 per cent, but it is up 17 per cent in tire non-vital areas such as office buildings, theatres and shopping plazas, not that these are not of genuine concern in our economy but they are not the areas of greatest thrust and where the greatest need is. More of our money and effort must be directed into housing and productive industrial facilities.
There is good and there is bad, but this budget and the determination of Canadians to make it work offer genuine hope. The budget gives an indication of total direction of government policies which are beginning to emerge. In the budget we have fiscal responsibility with a budgeted surplus, and a determined attack on inflation. The acceleration of the Kennedy round tariff reductions is an indication of the willingness of the government to break its way into a period of free trade, not without reservations, not without care, but with a genuine desire to do the things that will make us a truly great international trading nation.
The delay of tax incentives on construction that is not directly productive is going to put greater emphasis on housing, and will assist expansion in the less favoured areas of the country.
Other things have taken place outside the budget, Mr. Speaker. The Prices and Incomes Commission has been established. We have the new Regional Expansion Act, the Export
2918C-634J
The Budget-Mr. Danson Development Corporation, the N.H.A. amendments and the official languages bill. All these are tied into a package of expansion and international outlook and are based on a deep concern for national unity. Soon we will have our white paper on tax reform outlining proposals for major tax reforms and increasing our dialogue with the provinces on tax matters, something which perhaps we have neglected for too great a time in the past.
As the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour mentioned, we have the input from the Carter commission report which I hope will be reflected in the white paper on tax reform. If I might digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out how my hon. friends who call themselves the effective opposition-
I should say the defective opposition-accepted the Carter Commission report as the panacea, the answer to all the problems. They like to put things into neat little packages. If they do not have an answer they say, "Take Carter, take Watkins."
Sometimes we are not inclined to examine these things fully. But in going over this process of tax reform I must say I personally am beginning to realize the wisdom of many of the Carter concepts, some of which I was inclined to reject. As one looks at the complexities of our tax system, one comes to the conclusions that the Carter Commission arrived at-not all of them, but some of them. After two and a half years of sitting, the members of that commission realized it was not possible to improve our tax system- yes, possible to improve it a little, but it would be a band-aid approach. These were not wild-eyed radical men. They were sound business people, accountants, academics, and after two and a half years of trying to find a way to patch up our tax system they said it was necessary to change it. From my limited experience since I reached here, I am arriving at the same conclusion. Now, we have a genuine pattern of government policy that is beginning to emerge and that is setting the stage for the future.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
As I mentioned in my address on the debate on foreign ownership, I believe the week before last, there is a need for greater attention to training in management skills. At that time I did not have sufficient time to express my concern for the lack of a cohesive science policy or what I would like to call a policy of technological improvement in which we would have a much more freewheeling and openhanded approach to development,
June 11, 1969

The Budget-Mr. C. Stewart particularly among the smaller firms. There are some good programs under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and elsewhere, but I think they are too narrow and restrictive in their outlook. We need small companies, primarily Canadian owned, which will through research and development produce products of originality in areas where we have special interests or special expertise. In this way we could have an imaginative type of Canadian based industry which would be able to find its way into the export market because of its originality, skill, expertise and good design, without the crutch of high tariffs or subsidies.. This is the way we can make our country strong and increase our productivity, thus lessening the inflationary pressures.
There are other things we could do, but I shall not discuss them in this debate. When we speak of inflation many of us here, in all conscience, can speak of it with a genuine concern for improvement of the situation in respect of the senior citizens on fixed incomes.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then why don't you do something about it?

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think the government has a responsibility to set the example because we have a large number of senior civil servants, not all but many of whom are suffering. I hope they will receive a great deal more attention. In closing, may I say that I think this is a responsible imaginative budget and a solid achievement. The total legislation and the legislation surrounding it which I mentioned leads in a direction with which I can identify. Really the accomplishments of this government in a period of one year have been quite remarkable, particularly when one considers some of the delays we have experienced. What we have is a pattern which I think will give some thrust to Canadian development, particularly in the areas where it is needed. It is based on Canadian needs and concerns. It is one which, gives encouragement and, I believe, hope.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate on the budget because of my deep concern for western agriculture. The farmers of western Canada have waited patiently since the election of last June 25 for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) to announce a new agricultural policy. To date we have heard of none. The farmers have waited patiently for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) to 
announce new wheat sales which would get rid of the largest grain surplus in our history. To date we have heard of none. We listened last week to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) when he presented his budget, fully expecting him to announce a program of assistance to western agriculture. Again there was none. Has this government no concern for western Canada? How much longer do they expect our farmers to exist under the present conditions?
I would say the cash situation in western Canada is fast approaching the deplorable conditions we saw in the 1930's, and nobody wants those days back. The western farmer was able to survive that crisis. However, today we are in another world and the farmer has greater commitments to meet, such as property taxes, hydro, telephone, fertilizer, and farm machinery. Many of these things have tripled in price and then there is the large increase in daily living costs. Yes, the farmer survived the thirties. However, unless there is immediate cash assistance to the western farmer he will not survive the life of the present Liberal government.
Most legislation this government has passed pertaining to agriculture has placed greater hardships on the family farm operation. The dairy policy subsidizes the larger producer with no subsidy for the small operator or for the farmer who is just starting a herd. This government passed a new Farm Improvement Loans Act and a new Farm Credit Corporation Act, both of which increased the interest rate by 50 per cent. If a farmer makes a loan today he is lucky if he can pay the interest, let alone the principle.
In case a farmer survives all the hurdles this government has placed in front of him, this government came up with new estate tax policies which make it most difficult to continue a family farm operation. The farm policy of this government seems to be, "We will get you either way, dead or alive." This government has to take a more aggressive attitude to finding markets for grain. Why do we not have a special trade mission set up to deal exclusively with grain and see if we can recover some of our lost markets? We are all aware of the high quality of Canadian wheat, and surely there are markets when 80 per cent of the world population goes to bed hungry every night. The government has to show leadership to the Wheat Board and make a determined effort to move the grain.
The Wheat Board has announced a five bushel quota as the maximum most delivery
June 11, 1969

points will receive in western Canada for the crop year ending July 31. The farmers cannot exist on a five bushel quota and the government must realize this. This is why I say immediate action must be taken to move grain. The agriculture committee toured western Canada in April to get a first-hand look at the serious situation. The members of the committee returned to Ottawa and agreed conditions were not good. They tabled their report to the House of Commons over a month ago, and still there is no action from the government. I have just returned from western Canada and I can assure you the businessmen of most rural communities are feeling the effects of this situation. Because of their high accounts receivable position many are having a hard time to survive.
Because the whole economy of western Canada is in jeopardy I would ask the government to seriously consider an acreage payment of $10 per acre up to a maximum of 300 acres. A program of this type could be implemented with very little delay because all the information needed is in the farmers permit book. When the government spends large sums of money in eastern Canada, like the $100 million grant to Hull, surely they could consider an acreage payment for western farmers at this time. It is the one way to alleviate the serious cash shortage in the western agriculture economy.
I was sorry there was no increase in old age pensions announced in the budget. It is a disgrace for a nation like Canada to ask her senior citizens to live on $109 a month and retain their dignity. How many members of this house could exist on $109 a month? Old age pensions should be given top priority by the government so our senior citizens can participate in our so-called just society. Everybody talks about this problem at election time but we never see any action.
I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance on presenting a balanced budget. We in the province of Manitoba have had the satisfaction of our provincial government balancing the budget, so we realize how necessary it is during inflationary times such as we have now.
Again, I stress to this government the necessity for moving western grain. I quote from an article in the Winnipeg Tribune of June 7:
France has often been criticized by our government for undercutting our prices and the long lamented I.G.A., but they have shown much more initiative in disposing of their surplus stocks. This week they reached an agreement with the United Arab Republic to sell them 600,000 tons of wheat
The Budget-Mr. Gilbert
annually over a period of three years for a total of about 66,000,000 bushels, and they will make them a gift of 10,000,000 bushels.
We report this for what it is worth but it seems to us that a lesson could be learned from this that might benefit Canada as a whole; in other words, markets are still open for wheat around the world-at a price.
This article is by James Richardson and Sons. The government must develop policies that will sell our surplus grain. Lack of sales has created economic hardships for our farmers which threaten their survival. In closing I repeat my appeal to the government. Immediate action is necessary in the form of acreage payments and top priority must be given to selling western grain.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) would be present this afternoon, but he is probably on more important business. I had hoped that his parliamentary secretary would be here so that we could have a dialogue on the objectives that were presented in arguments presented by members on this side. The budget is more expressive in respect of what it does than in what it intended to do. The Minister of Finance has a fixation for balanced budgets, services and employment. He adopts the attitude of what a good boy am I, by patting himself on the back and suggesting he has a surplus of $250 million for the 1969-70 fiscal year. Of course, he does not mention that in solving the problem his way he is hitting hard the wrong groups within this country. He is not worried about the ordinary wage earners, the pensioners or the veterans. He actually helps the people in the upper income groups.
This really underlines the economic conservatism of the Minister of Finance, which is only surpassed by that of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp). It is quite obvious that he is preaching for a call. One would think he may be preaching for a call to the other place, but really he is preaching for a call to join the corporate elite because he feels he would like to be a second Robert Winters. Robert Winters really represents the corporate elite and the Minister of Finance wants to join him. He wants to join him to protect the interests of this group.
The Minister of Finance used the phrase in the budget speech "bogeyman of inflation". The support he got from the government side makes me think that the Minister of Finance

June 11, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Gilbert is like Moses, leading the people out of the wilderness into the promised land. When I heard the hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens) say that this was an exciting and interesting budget speech, and when I heard the hon. member for York North (Mr. Dan-son) say how proud he was in respect of this particular budget speech and then proceed to make a motherhood speech in which he indicated his concern about pensioners and those people on low incomes, I could only think that last night the members of this party gave them an opportunity to express their concern. In fact, we gave all members of the Liberal party an opportunity to do so through our subamendment which stated that no income tax would be payable by single persons with incomes below $2,000 a year or married persons with incomes below $4,000 per year. They expressed their concern for the people last night by voting against the subamendment.
For this reason, I suggest these members have changed from great reformists, as they pretended in their speeches, to great apologists on the part of the government. I hope that when the hon. member for York West and other members from Toronto suburbs return to their constituencies they will report they voted against the sub-amendment, as supported by members of the Conservative party, which indicated our concern for the people in low income brackets.
When we talk about inflation one would think that the minister and government members would define what they mean by inflation. They might well say it really fits within the classical definition of too many dollars in relation to too few goods, or vice versa. They might mention that the inflation record of Canada is not bad in comparison with other countries, more especially the United Kingdom and some European countries. They might even mention that the government is using ordinary instruments in respect of fighting inflation by increasing interest rates and by creating a so-called slack in the economy, or by preaching for greater productivity.
In any event, these people fail to mention that at the moment we appear to be suffering from a conspiracy on the part of financial institutions in respect of the money market which exists in Canada and elsewhere within the world. The Minister of Finance set forth some solutions. He said to Canadians that he was not going to impose any more taxes on .them but was not going to lift the two per

cent social development tax he imposed last October. He also said he was going to extend by one year the 3 per cent surtax he imposed until the end of 1970. Surely, if there is any increase in tax it is with regard to that extension in respect of the surtax.
The Minister of Finance said he was going to raise $25 million in the year 1969 by holding onto that surtax, and that in 1970 he would have obtained $155 million. If I were to accept that phrase of the hon. member for York West, that this was an exciting and interesting budget, I would point out to the hon. member some of the exciting and interesting things the government might have done. The government could have implemented one of the recommendations of the Carter report which indicated that the mining and petroleum companies were getting tax advantages in respect of tax holidays and incentive taxes. When I asked the assistant deputy minister, at the time the estimates in respect of natural resources were being considered, how much money our mining and petroleum companies got out of Canada by way of tax holidays and tax incentives each year, he quoted the figure of $150 million as of 1964. This would more than take care of the decrease in revenue if the 3 per cent surtax were eliminated.
The assistant deputy minister also said that of that $150 million granted to these petroleum and mining companies, 85 per cent went to eight large companies, composed of five large mining companies and three petroleum companies. About 60 per cent of this 85 per cent relates to mining companies, and 65 per cent went to petroleum companies which are foreign owned. You can see that a substantial amount of the $150 million given by way of tax relief is going directly into the hands of foreign owners. You must realize that little or no money in this regard is going into the pockets of Canadians.
If the hon. member wants to bring forth some exciting and interesting things he might have recommended a capital gains tax. This has been advocated not only by the Carter commission but by many members within his own party. He made no mention of the control of interest rates. I understand he has said outside of the house that the interest rates in Canada are outrageous. We in this party say they are unconscionable.
We believe there is a conspiracy by financial institutions in respect of interest rates around the world. This is true when we think of N.H.A. rates which will probably increase
June 11, 1969

June 11, 1969
The Budget-Mr. Gilbert received. But if the hon. member is preaching for a call, he had better walk lightly on those two touchy subjects.
If the minister had really wanted a budget that was exciting and interesting, he would have spoken about rolling back the interest rate on housing. He would have brought forth the fact that the last report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation indicated that as of the end of April the corporation had a decline of 57 per cent in their investment in housing across the country. He would also have indicated that as of the end of April the insurance companies had a decline of 20 per cent in their investment in housing. This is the type of thing I hoped the Minister of Finance would have dealt with and which would have been supported by the hon. member for York West. If he wanted the budget to be exciting and interesting, the hon. member for York West would have said that the Canadian Welfare Council has pointed out that we should build between 20,000 and 30,000 public housing units in Canada, and we should apply to them a low interest rate which would make them attractive. Instead of this he was strangely silent. I assume he is content with the past high interest rate and low production of public housing units.
Those are the three main areas the Minister of Finance dealt with in his budget. What is it that his budget does not do? It does little or nothing with regard to the plight of the agricultural industry. The minister made no mention of cash payments to farmers who are short of cash. He made no mention of acreage payments. I would wager my bottom dollar that when the government is prepared to make a statement on agriculture it will wait until the house recesses so that it cannot receive the criticism due to it as a result of its do-nothing policy in agriculture.
What has the minister done to solve the problem of unemployment? The unemployment figure was 4.8 per cent in 1968 and 4.8 per cent is projected for 1969. Speaking in numbers, this means between 400,000 and 450,000 people. Speaking in terms of regional unemployment, it means the unemployment rate in Ontario is 3.7 per cent; 8.4 per cent in Quebec and 10.5 per cent in the maritimes. When I hear the hon. member for York West say that anything over 6 per cent represents a serious condition, I realize he has done little or nothing to study the problem of unemployment. The Economic Council of Canada has said that anything between 2 per cent and 3 per cent represents a serious problem. If the 
hon. member for York West had known that, he would not have made the statement that he did. The hon. member should realize that the burden of inflation is being placed upon the backs of the unemployed of Canada. Between 20 per cent and 25 per cent of Canadians live below the poverty line; yet little or nothing has been done to solve this problem.
If the minister had wanted something really interesting and exciting in the budget he would have spoken in terms of instituting a guaranteed annual income. He would have said that people in certain areas of the country are entitled to an income which takes care of their basic needs. There may be differences with regard to different regions of Canada, but we would have set about settling those differences.
If we had a really avant garde Minister of Finance he would have spoken in terms of planned unemployment, because as we advance in technology we must advance in respect of our social concerns regarding people who are unemployed. We have to establish for them a base from which they are provided with the basic needs of society. I hope the government does not talk in terms of creating slack in the economy in order to tackle the problem of unemployment. I hope it talks in terms of a guaranteed annual income to take care of people who have been affected by the disparities within the country, and in terms of some of the problems which will occur as a result of technological advance.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
One final item with which the Minister of Finance did not deal concerns the erosion of Canadian independence. The only statement on this subject in the house was that he intended to make a statement in connection with the Royal Securities Company before the session adjourns. He did not attempt to tackle this question of Canadian independence. I had the opportunity of addressing the high school students at the Eastern Commerce High School in my riding on Monday. They, themselves, drew attention to some of the facets of the Watkins report. A group of high school students is studying the report-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I thank members of the house for their indulgence. These students pointed out that $34 billion of foreign capital is presently within the Canadian economy in the form of equity ownership. They appreciate the difference between the continentalism expressed by members of the cabinet and the economic nationalism which was expressed by Hon. Walter Gordon. I had to say to them that Walter Gordon is dead as far as the Liberal party is concerned. They are treating him in the same way as they treated Judy LaMarsh. One of the ways in which to treat a person who has new ideas is to ignore him. They ignored Judy LaMarsh and they are attempting to ignore Walter Gordon. Well, Mr. Gordon still makes speeches in different places pleading for economic nationalism, though I believe he appreciates some of the difficulties which arise in connection with his "buy back Canada" plan and is prepared to make changes. The only newspaper in Canada which is making an attempt to present this question to Canadian readers is the Toronto Star which is supporting Mr. Gordon.
I would suggest to Mr. Gordon that as far as the Liberal party is concerned he is dead. Maybe we should invite him into the New Democratic party so that he may better present his ideas on economic nationalism and foreign ownership to the Canadian people. I appreciate that Mr. Gordon represents a group in Canada which may not share the ideas of the New Democratic party. Nevertheless, in order that this subject may be directed to the attention of all Canadians, it may be that Mr. Gordon should join our party and set forth his views on foreign ownership. My suggestion to the Star is that one of the best ways in which to tackle foreign ownership is through an indirect approach by way of persuading Canadians to urge reform of the electoral laws of Canada. It is only when a government makes money available to members of the different parties that members of those parties can exercise independent judgment with regard to the issues which face Canada.
Liberal members, and sometimes Conservative members, find it very difficult when they receive campaign moneys from the corporate elite, to tackle those circles on the question of corporate and foreign ownership. Maybe the Star should embark on a crusade to reform

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Is not corporate money as honest as trade union money for election purposes?

speechtext: Thank you. I am very glad the hon. member asked that question. He should realise that when the corporations give money for political purposes they do not ask the shareholders whether they should give the money to the Liberal party or to the Conservative party. There is no control whatsoever. But when it comes to trade union support of the New Democratic party-

-there is a voluntary checkoff in respect of money given. If we study the 1965 election returns, we find that the Liberal party received $2.6 millions toward their election campaign,, that the Tory party received $1.7 million and that the N.D.P. received $500,000. These are the facts according to the election returns, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Cote) would really look into the situation if they were not the correct returns, since he is very keen about collecting revenue. This is the picture, and I invite Liberal members to tell us just where they got that $2.6 million. If they did not get it from the corporate elite, from where did they get it and to whom are they responsible now they have received it? This is why I say we must change the electoral laws, and I am asking the Toronto Star and other newspapers across Canada to launch a campaign in order that members may not be dependent on money received from these corporations.
In closing I say again that the budget is a hoax when it comes to advancing a just society. I trust that all the Liberal members who have realized just what a hoax it is will take immediate steps to see that some of the solutions which members of the New Democratic party, and also of the Conservative party, have proposed are put into effect.

speechtext:
The hon. member says "Hear, hear." I would remind him that in this country we have a high standard of living. Indeed, we have reached a point at which workers in some of our trades can go on strike demanding wage increases in excess of a dollar an hour.
The budget about which we have had an opportunity of thinking and talking recognizes one very basic point with regard to the development of Canada as a nation, a diverse nation which extends from the Atlantic to the Arctic and to the Pacific. It recognizes that there are regions of Canada which are disadvantaged; that there are people who suffer from lack of education and lack of economic opportunity. The budget recognizes, too, that many of our first inhabitants, the Indians and the Eskimos, have a long way to go before they reach a level of economic activity such as one might reasonably expect in Canada. The budget recognizes that there is regional disparity in Canada and I am hoping that in the implementation of the statements outlined by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and his colleague the Minister of Regional and Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), northern Canada can share in some of the programs and ideas which have been advanced.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I should like for a moment to outline what I believe are some of the regional disparities in that area of Canada that lies north of the 60th parallel. The basic problem in that region is the high cost of living caused by extraneous factors such as transportation costs, communications, cold and long winters and, equally important, the general lack of understanding that the rest of Canada, including some people in the financial community, have with respect to the potential of northern Canada.
We have seen in the field of housing during the past four or five years a very exciting program that has provided the Eskimo people in the north with approximately 1,000 new homes. By the end of this contruction season I would expect every Eskimo family in Canada north of the 60th parallel to have a decent standard of housing, including proper sanitation facilities and power. I might add that these houses are not gifts but are part of a

rental housing program that has brought great benefit to the Eskimo communities in the north.
If I may digress for a moment, I observe the minister responsible for this particular program in the house this afternoon. In addition to saying to him that I think this was one of the great accomplishments of his ministry in Indian Affairs and Northern Development, as recognition of his services to the North, the government of the Northwest Territories is tomorrow dedicating their new office building in Yellowknife to the minister and calling it the "Arthur Laing Building".

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: When is he going to the Senate?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
One of our housing problems is that in developed areas of the north, particularly in the Mackenzie valley, it is virtually impossible today to obtain funds, either through government agencies such as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or from financial institutions, for mortgage purposes. For example, in Yellowknife where the territorial government contracted for the construction of about 16 homes for their employees, the successful bidder, a highly respected construction company in western Canada, had at last reports still been unable to find the necessary mortgage money.
Some areas of northern Canada are presently experiencing an unparalleled economic boom, and these areas include Yellowknife, Inuvik and Hay River. However, people, including the government in certain instances as I have illustrated, are finding it increasingly difficult to obtain the necessary money to go ahead with the construction of housing in order to make the north attractive to prospective residents. The situation is getting serious and development of the north is being held back at the present time.
Another area of disparity concerns the small businessman who is attempting to create for himself his own little financial empire, be it in the form of a gas station, motel or small aircraft charter or aircraft repair company. The Industrial Development Bank has from time to time made forays into the north and provided some form of financial assistance to northern businessmen. Its terms and conditions in the north are much more stringent than is the case in the south; and, for the information of hon. members, when I refer to the south I mean that part of the country below the 60th parallel.
June 11, 1969

The Industrial Development Bank has applied these stringent conditions to the point where any small businessman who wishes to develop an idea or proposal finds it very difficult to obtain the sort of financing he requires to establish himself in business. Each of these small businesses depends, of course, on local custom and patronage, and the cumulative effect of the activities of a small business can be one of the answers to the problem of local employment.
However, there is a glimmer of hope, Mr. Speaker, and that glimmer of hope is that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), in conjunction with his officials, announced last February the establishment of a small business development loan fund for businessmen in the north. The creation of such a fund is a start. According to the publicity, approximately $5 million will be provided over a period of time. In effect, the fund will provide $300,000 each to both the Yukon and Northwest Territories in any one year. Unfortunately, before the fund can be used regulations have to be promulgated and credit committees established. Consequently, it will have no direct effect on the economy in the north during the coming year.
Another area of disparity in the north is in the cost of supplying electric power. The average cost of power in a small community in the north with diesel plants in operation is about 12 cents per kilowatt hour. This means that a family in a community living in a house with three or four electrical outlets pays anywhere between $30 and $50 a month for power. Even more important is the effect of this high cost of power on the local business community. For example, in a number of communities merchants are required to pay approximately $1,000 a month on average for electric power. This means they must charge extra for their goods and services, and the people in the community are already paying high costs.
If I had time I should like to elaborate at length on the cost of electric power in the north. I should also like to speak about what I believe is the very silly provision contained in the Northern Canada Power Commission act that each of its establishments must pay its own way. There is no way of establishing a power grid and thus reducing costs in one community at the expense of a larger community or area of economic development. I hope that this legislation will soon come before parliament in order that this particular provision can be changed.
The Budget-Mr. Orange One of the criticisms of this budget is directed at the proposed 3 per cent tax on air fares. Hon. members will appreciate that the aeroplane is the mode of travel in northern Canada, just as it is in the northern areas of the provinces. I should like to put on record a telegram that is addressed to me, one of many that I have received from northern residents, which reads as follows:
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The Northwest Territories Tourist Association is expressing the views of all residents of the north in asking that the proposed tax on air transportation not be levied for any transportations to or from any point north of the sixtieth parallel. We feel since air transportation is a necessity in the northern communities that the tax will be discriminatory and add to the already burdensome cost of living in the north.
With the exception of the central Arctic, air fares in the north generally have been increased. Pacific Western Air Lines Limited uses the municipal airport in downtown Edmonton. Recently, Pacific Western Air Lines added a $1 per passenger landing or takeoff fee with respect to flights beginning or ending at Edmonton Municipal Airport. At Easter time Pacific Western Air Lines increased its tariff for passengers and freight by approximately 10 per cent. The north depends almost totally on air transport; by adding to the transportation costs of the people in the north the government will be creating a situation leading to disparity. That is what the tax on air travel will do. When the minister examines the effect of this additional tax, I hope at the same time he will examine the effect the tax will have on the various regions of Canada. What effect will it have, for example, on the small mining exploration company that is working in the north? What will the tax do to the family which wishes to go south on leave or for holidays during the summer. What will be its effect on Indian people who wish to take aircraft out to their camps when they go on spring hunts. I suggest that only about 5 per cent, or at most 10 per cent, of all air traffic in the north is non-government air traffic. The net effect of this particular tax therefore will be very small.
I could talk about many other subjects, but I shall limit myself to one or two that are important. I have talked before in the house about the problems our Indian and Eskimo peoples face with respect to the price they obtain for their fur skins. I know that this matter has been studied at various times by officials in the Department of Indians Affairs

June 11. 1983
The Budget-Mr. Orange and Northern Development. The product, if we may call it that, we are here considering fluctuates greatly in price. It is most difficult to obtain. The life of the trapper and hunter is hard and often unrewarding. Notwithstanding these difficulties, these people like living in the bush or on the tundra. Our trapper incurs ever increasing costs, but he is not given the tax relief available to other producers in our economy. For instance, he must pay sales tax on his skidoo, his rifle and his gasoline. Unless we do something to stabilize the fur market and fur prices we shall perpetuate for generations to come a welfare situation. Sometimes a man goes into the bush after game and he is successful in the hunt. Yet sometimes he obtains only enough fur to pay for his trip. Not enough is left over for the support of his family. The problem lies in the wildly fluctuating prices of furs. Nevertheless, there are people who wish to continue with their trapping and hunting and they have a right to do so. We should encourage those who want to live that way to carry on with what they are doing. Some may argue that furs are luxuries and that the government should not support the fur trade. Furs may be luxuries for fashion models in Toronto, Montreal or New York, but to the trappers they are a means of support. When we develop our regional economic programs, I hope the government will look at the fur trade. Many depend on it. I hope that some device will be created as a result of which the people concerned, the Indians, Eskimos and trappers, can look forward to stable lives. They have a right to that.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I wish to touch on the subject of education. Notwithstanding the many excellent programs which have been introduced into the north during the last
15 years, and one could enumerate advances in education, in economic development, in economic growth as well as many other advances, the overriding necessity the government must face is the necessity of consulting the local people of the north. I am referring to those who were born in the north. I think I have previously referred to the sparkling example of the program undertaken in Frobisher Bay. The government decided to build a regional high school in that area and young people in communities 200, 500 or 700 miles from it are to attend. By and large our Eskimo people seem happy about the high school. They want their children to be educated. Many of them do not know why a high school cannot be built in their own local communities. In my hand I have a communication from the Igloolik Community Association. That community, as hon. members well know, is in the Northwest Territories. The president of the association says in his letter that the people of Igloolik disagree with the concept of having to send their children to a high school hundreds of miles away. Actually, their chief complaint is that they were not consulted about this matter. So, once again I say that consultation is most important.
I will, therefore, conclude on this note, Mr. Speaker. Although we have introduced many excellent programs into the north and although much progress is being made, we must never forget that there must be continuing consultation with those who were born in the north. I am talking about the Indian and Eskimo peoples.
